Grade 2 · Unit 2-C

Land and Water, Fast and Slow

How does land change fast and slow, and where is water found?

The land around us is always changing, sometimes in a day and sometimes over thousands of years. This unit looks at quick and slow changes, how wind and water move soil and sand and what slows them down, and where water is found as liquid or ice.

In this lesson

  1. Earth events can be quick or slow
  2. Slowing wind and water
  3. Where water is; solid or liquid
  4. Try it at home
  5. Check yourself
  6. Play: Guard the Sand

Concept 1

Earth events can be quick or slow

Some changes to land happen fast, like floods and volcanoes; others happen slowly, like erosion and canyon carving.

Analogy

Some changes are fast like a door slamming. Some are slow like a crayon wearing down. Door slam = a flood or a volcano: done quickly. Crayon wearing down = a canyon or a dune: it takes a very long time, a little at a time.

“Some changes are quick. Some are slow.”

Diagram

Erosion means moving soil, sand, or rock by wind or water. A dune is a hill of sand that wind has piled up.

Picture pairs for the sort: a flood (before and after), a volcano, a canyon, and a dune. Point to each one and ask: did this happen fast or slow?

“Fast: flood moved soil. Slow: water carved rock.”

Try it

Sort the six picture cards into fast or slow. Then name the Earth material on each card: water, soil, sand, or rock.

The picture cards show a flood, a volcano, an earthquake, a canyon, a dune, and soil forming.

“I see a volcano. It is fast.”

Data

Class evidence chart. Sample evidence:

EventClueFast or slow?Earth material
FloodMoved soil in one nightFastSoil, water
Volcano eruptionNew rock and ash appeared quicklyFastRock
EarthquakeRoad cracked quicklyFastRock, soil
CanyonRiver carved rock over many yearsSlowRock, water
DuneSand moved a little each yearSlowSand
Soil formingTiny rock pieces changed over many yearsSlowSoil

“Earthquake: fast. Dune moves: slow.”

Concept 2

Slowing wind and water

Wind and moving water can move soil and sand; plants, rocks, and barriers can help.

Try it

A barrier is something that blocks or slows movement.

Fan air gently over dry sand or soil with a folded card; pour a little water. Add grass, sticks, or stones and test again.

Measure how far the sand moves in finger widths. A finger width is how wide one of your fingers is, about 1 to 2 centimeters (a bit under an inch). Measure one finger with a ruler and write it on your tray card.

“Wind moved sand. Grass helped stop it.”

One messy trial is not the finding: fan or pour three times for each guard and compare the tries before you choose.

Data

Sand moved, in finger widths, for 3 tries each (sample data, made up for practice):

  • No guard: 4, 5, 4
  • Grass: 1, 1, 2

Draw your own tries in a chart or table next to these. Then finish this sentence: Grass moved ___ sand than no guard.

“No guard: sand moved 4 to 5 finger widths. Grass: sand moved only 1 to 2 finger widths.”

Real world

Beach grass helps hold dunes. It grows on dunes along Lake Michigan, such as Sleeping Bear Dunes.

“Beach grass holds sand.”

Concept 3

Where water is; solid or liquid

Water is found in lakes, rivers, oceans, ice, snow, clouds, and underground; it can be liquid or solid.

Diagram

Liquid water flows, like water in a lake. Solid water keeps its shape, like ice and snow.

A map of Michigan with the Great Lakes around it and clouds in the sky. The list under the picture shows where to find solid and liquid water.

  • Solid: snow, ice
  • Liquid: lakes, rivers, underground water
  • Clouds: tiny drops of water or tiny ice crystals floating in the air

“Water is in lakes, rivers, snow, and ice.”

Try it

Sort the six pictures into solid water or liquid water.

The six cards are snow, an ice cube, ice on a lake, a lake, a river, and a glass of water.

“Snow: solid. Lake: liquid.”

Data

Sample class results

PlaceSolid or liquid?
LakeLiquid
RiverLiquid
Underground waterLiquid
SnowSolid
IceSolid

Make your own chart: list each place you find water, and write solid or liquid next to it.

“We found water in 5 places.”

Real world

Earth resources are things from Earth that people use, like water, soil, trees, rocks, and sand. Michigan farms grow food in soil, with water from rain.

“Farms use soil and water.”

Hands-on · Design or investigate

Try it at home or in class

Erosion Guard Test. Problem: wind or water moves sand in the tray. Students compare a tray with no guard to trays with a guard of their choice: grass, stones, or a paper barrier. They test each guard 3 times with the same fan or pour, measure sand movement, and choose the better solution using evidence.

Data

Sample results (made up for practice)

GuardTry 1Try 2Try 3
No guard454
Grass112
Stones212
Paper barrier332

Numbers are finger widths of sand moved. One finger width is about 1 to 2 centimeters.

Try it

What you need

  • a tray
  • sand or soil
  • a small cup or dropper
  • grass clippings, twigs, stones, or paper barriers
  • a folded card for fanning
  • picture cards or printed photos
  • a ruler
  • paper

Safety: Wash hands after sand/soil trays. Do not blow on sand. Use a folded card to fan it and keep sand away from faces and eyes. No coin cells or magnets are required.

What you do

1. Fast or slow (10 minutes). Sort picture cards into fast and slow changes, and name the Earth material.

2. Erosion Guard Test (30 minutes). Put sand in a tray. Fan it gently with a folded card, with no guard, then with grass, stones, or a barrier. Measure how far the sand moved in finger widths (about 1 to 2 centimeters each). Do each 3 times.

3. Solid or liquid (10 minutes). Sort water pictures and make a chart of where you find water.

No time or no good weather? Use this data

Words to know

land
the solid part of Earth’s surface.
water
liquid found in lakes, rivers, and oceans. Frozen water is ice or snow.
fast
happens in a short time.
slow
happens over a long time.
erosion
moving soil, sand, or rock by wind or water.
dune
a hill of sand that wind has piled up.
barrier
something that blocks or slows movement.
map
a drawing that shows places.
solid
keeps its shape, like ice.
liquid
flows, like water.
resource
something from Earth that people use, like water, soil, trees, rocks, and sand.
Tutor notes: misconceptions, pacing

Pacing: 5 sessions of 30 minutes.

Common misconceptions to listen for:

  • “Land never changes.” Correct: land changes fast and slow.
  • “Only earthquakes and volcanoes change land.” Correct: wind, water, and ice also change land, often slowly.
  • “Wind is just clouds moving.” Correct: wind is moving air.
  • “Water is only in lakes.” Correct: water is also in rivers, ice, snow, clouds, and underground.

Limits and cautions:

  • Sand/soil trays require handwashing and gentle fanning rules.
  • Quick events like floods or earthquakes should be taught calmly; focus on evidence and preparation, not fear.
  • If an extension uses lights or magnets, use ready-made lamps only and keep magnets away from Chromebooks.

You did this before / what is new: New in grade 2: you test wind and water on sand with repeated trials, and you compare erosion-guard solutions with data. Earlier units tested plants and pushes; here the new variable is the guard you place on the sand, and the new measurement is finger widths of sand moved. This is the first guard test in the series; later units count spoonfuls of sediment from different trays, so do not compare those numbers with these.
